title: Desportes to Aldobrandini
subtitle: A warning to Rome, hidden in plain sight.
intro: Desportes explains his silence, attacks failed promises of support and defends Mayenne. Ordinary handwriting gives way to cipher—and returns whenever the writer chooses.
status: The body text is readable throughout, with disclosed editorial restorations.

english.text: If I have not written to His Holiness and to Your Most Illustrious Lordship as often as duty commands, two things have prevented me. The first is that it is difficult to tell the truth without someone among them finding his interests affected. The other is that affairs are handled by so many hands, with such different passions, that we are in such uncertainty that our destruction seems inevitable. The prospect of our loss could not fail to cause His Holiness extreme displeasure, and I shall avoid, as far as I can, being the bearer of bad news. Thus I had resolved to write no more to him or to Your Most Illustrious Lordship, had your letter of 1 June not assured me that His Holiness had welcomed the very particular account I ventured to give him of events here, and my freely telling him what I thought of them.

Although many new things have happened since my letters, Your Lordship will find that in fact I was not mistaken, and that people would not remedy matters in time, either when I was over there or since. In the end, unless God intervenes, I see the cause of the Catholic religion in this kingdom in a bad way, for several reasons I could tell Your Most Illustrious Lordship, beyond what I explain to His Holiness on the subject. Moreover, everything he is told by those who have exercised that ministry here for the Holy See seems to be treated as so many oracles, leaving no credit for the truth—which will now be found to be as I have always stated it, at the risk of my head. From Monsieur Mateouci down to the present state of things, they alone have brought more ruin to affairs than the enemies have, so full have they been of I know not what that does not suit us, or of little experience of our dispositions, and of passion.

And if I have put anything forward in the account I am giving His Holiness about the conduct of the said Mateuci, the slightest letter anyone might write to me will always bring me to appear wherever they wish, to maintain it to his face. As for Monsieur de Malvoisie, I was not there when he and Mayenne fell into discord. Nevertheless, the legate’s nephew has complained to me of it; besides, it is difficult to contradict a general report.

Your Lordship can also consider for yourself that the King of Spain’s army has done nothing but remain on the frontier, bringing disgrace upon so great a monarch, and has withdrawn merely at a rumour that Navarre was coming to seek it out. Furthermore, the legate, without any consideration whatever, wants us to proceed to the election of a king just when the enemy is beginning to win the voices of many who were his enemies, through his appearance of wishing to become Catholic, and is to attend Mass on Sunday.

Having nothing with which to resist him except promises by which we have been so often deceived, we would need many deeds before we could be made to reject the prospect of peace. It will be no small achievement if we temper it into a truce. Everyone is tired of being a laughingstock to all Christendom, and of seeing themselves abandoned, only to end by breathing their last. As for promises, our enemies are not without them: they offer to show letters from Your Most Illustrious Lordship concerning his reception if he becomes Catholic.

The Holy See is weary of continuing its expenditure, which one may say amounted to something during the pontificate of Pope Gregory. But since then it would have been better for it had we been denied all hope of aid outright, so that we might take a definite resolution. Let Your Most Illustrious Lordship only remember how insistently I asked for a member of the House of Bourbon, and the refusal I received; then for the Infanta’s marriage to one of our princes. I was refused outright, the matter being referred to the legate and the Duke of Feria.

I think I made it quite clear that we would never hazard our religion, honours and lives without firmer assurances, and unless His Holiness spoke more plainly. We want assurances from him alone, as the party most concerned; otherwise we should not be in a position to do better in future than in the past. I would have been very imprudent not to act otherwise, knowing the Spaniards as I do. That made me reject the candidate proposed to me by His Holiness, who in truth would have been the best; but one needed a clear and certain prospect. Even if my master had been willing to let himself be drawn into it, no one would have resisted him more than I. And where would he be now?

The enemies still offer to show a letter from His Holiness to the legate, instructing him to do nothing to the prejudice of the House of Bourbon, against the fundamental laws of the kingdom, or against the Catholics who support Navarre—something very contrary to so many assurances made to me. I have said it, and shall say it until I die: if harm comes of it, people have willed it so. We have not failed to point out everything possible, having no passion other than religion.

Yet we remain amid these uncertainties while the others take advantage of the opportunity. Are they not doing well? For all our pains I still expect a world of reproaches, all falling upon Mayenne, who does more than he ought without any fear; for honour is worth more than all the appearances sought by most men, and the end will crown the work. For, at a time when everyone is banded together to tear apart our State—which would then bring the ruin of Christendom—abandoned by everyone, all his warnings disregarded, and mocked over them by people who, apart from being ministers of a great prince, would not be above the rank or of too good a family to serve as servants, he takes heart against every kind of tempest. He works to provide the supreme and sole remedy, his presence, to prevent the imminent fall of the State and religion.

There can be no doubt that some will wish, as is their custom, to cover their malice with a world of falsehoods. But if their design has been made vain, there is no lack of people able to write good defences. They will make the shame people would cast upon faces marked only by honour and magnanimity fall back upon its authors. Would to God that His Holiness knew as I do how his ministers have behaved, their self-interest, and that of those who present themselves as nothing but religious, when there is only pure ambition, all too evident despite countless protestations to the contrary. There would have been no means of answering for it had the legate not intervened, in a matter in which His Holiness’s honour has been greatly implicated.

I speak of these affairs to Your Most Illustrious Lordship at great length. Indeed, if I did not fear importuning you, there would be enough to fill eight times as much paper. To avoid being too tedious, I shall say that if you knew, as I do, the artifice of our friends, what they have and do, their weakness, how the legate has shown himself their partisan in tearing apart our poor State to the detriment of the Holy See’s honour, and a world of other things, you would marvel a thousand times over at Mayenne’s patience.

That patience has extended even to being willing to accept Monsieur Guise as king, provided they showed him how he could be defended. But they want us to believe mere words, as though there were any prospect of giving further trust to people who have never shown us any, and whose guiding principle is to deceive us.

Perhaps you will even find it strange that I have drawn your attention to the two points the enemies are circulating, both about His Holiness’s letter and about yours in particular. But it seems to me right that Your Lordship should know everything, so that you can provide for it. It is true, as I have declared often enough, that if His Holiness is pleased to communicate his intentions for Mayenne through me, without interposing the legate, Mayenne will take only His Holiness’s commands as his rule.

Besides, things have reached such a pass between them that, were it not for respect for His Holiness, the legate would no longer play for so long at Mayenne’s expense, or with the ruin of everyone in his household. Indeed, he has been so disrespectful that he has made him fear being in His Holiness’s disfavour. Everyone nevertheless thinks this is a device to achieve his designs and oblige the Spaniard, which has always been his principal aim.

Illustrissimo Monseigneur,
Je supplie très humblement le Créateur donner à Votre Seigneurie Illustrissime très heureuse et très longue vie. De Paris ce [22] juillet 1593.
D. V. S. I.
Très humble et très obéissant servit[eur],
Desportes.

closing.english:
Most Illustrious Lord,
I most humbly beseech the Creator to grant Your Most Illustrious Lordship a very happy and very long life. Paris, [22] July 1593.
D. V. S. I.
Your very humble and very obedient servant,
Desportes.

regions.reading: Je supplie tres humblement le Createur donner à Vostre Seigneurie Illustrissime tres heureuse et tres longue vie. De Paris ce [22] juillet 1593.
D. V. S. I. — original courtesy abbreviation retained.
Tres humble et tres obeissant servit[eur]

notes.title: One sign, two letters
body: The alphabet was already reconstructed by S. Tomokiyo. Eleven ordinary signs each allow two letters: A/N, B/O, C/P, D/Q, E/R, F/S, G/T, H/U, I/X, L/Y and M/Z. The work here was to read these particular manuscripts accurately and choose the letters that make the French, rather than to invent a new alphabet.

Hovering a cipher mark shows the family allowed by the key and the selected reading in this passage. I/J and U/V follow early spelling conventions. A whole-word sign can represent QUE, QUI or POUR; other abbreviations and designations require their own evidence.

The key explains why a perfectly legible sign may still need context. Three consecutive E/R signs are three choices, not three missing letters. The small key samples below come from the manuscripts; they are not a modern font substituted for the handwriting.

notes.title: The g-like sign means “legate”
body: The g-like code was read against an aligned cipher and contemporary readable copy as le légat. It is not merely the personal initial of a mysterious “Monsieur G.” The legate is identified as Filippo Sega, Cardinal of Piacenza, whose tenure and correspondence fit July 1593.

The surrounding title signs are read in their local settings: Monsieur, Sa Sainteté, and other courtesy forms must not all be forced into one universal expansion. The exact lettering of an expanded title is different from recovering ordinary alphabetic cipher signs.

A spare E/R-family sign before LEGAT in the Frachetta letter is retained in the apparatus. It does not put the title or Sega’s identity back in doubt. Desportes’s allegations remain his allegations, not independently proved facts merely because the text is readable.

notes.title: Two letters, one day
body: The accepted date for both letters is 22 July 1593. A contemporary abstract in BnF français 3983, f. 141v, entries 13–14, names Desportes’s letters to Pietro Aldobrandini and Girolamo Frachetta and gives the date.

The closing displays [22] to distinguish that documentary date from a claim to read every stroke of the handwritten day numeral. The abstract is evidence for date and attribution, not a supplied plaintext of the cipher.

images.caption: Entry 13 names the Aldobrandini letter and dates it 22 July 1593.
Entry 14 names Frachetta and gives the same date.

notes.title: These lines were never encrypted
body: The Aldobrandini opening is ordinary French handwriting. Clear phrases continue to interrupt the cipher farther down the letter. Their difficulty comes from the hand, old spelling and contractions, rather than substitution.

The manuscript view includes those passages exactly as photographed. Connected cursive phrases are annotated as shared regions: they are not divided into artificial, supposedly exact character boxes. Their complete reading is available on hover and click. Cipher symbols, by contrast, have individual hit regions.

The French view modernizes spelling, I/J and U/V, and expands accepted courtesy abbreviations. It keeps the original wording and older turns of phrase. Punctuation and word division are editorial. The line inspector also gives the accepted reading in historical spelling.

notes.title: The legate’s nephew has a name
body: Girolamo Agucchi is accepted as the historical identification of the legate’s nephew. The British Library’s Agocchi correspondence catalogue supplies both the family relationship to Sega and April 1593 dealings with Mayenne and Malvasia.

A named April 1593 BnF letter supplies a clearer Hieronimo Agocchi subscription. The July 26 letter’s account of the Malvasia dispute adds the close contemporary setting. These sources converge on the person; they do not independently certify every complaint reported by Desportes.
Malvoisie is plausibly Innocenzo Malvasia. Mateouci / Mateuci is plausibly Girolamo Matteucci. These historical suggestions remain distinct from the accepted spellings in the text.

refs.label: British Library, Add MS 6875, especially items 31, 34–36

notes.title: A tiny sign with a written answer above it
body: In “pontificat du … Gregoire,” the lambda-shaped sign means PAPE. The strongest evidence is not simply that “Pope Gregory” makes sense. Earlier manuscripts put the word pape directly above the same shape.
One control reads AU FEU [PAPE] GREGOIR. FEU has its own three signs, so the code is not “feu pape.” The target spells GREGOIRE with one more final E than that control.

Three glossed occurrences were checked: two in one letter and a third in another. They are three occurrences in two letters, not three independent plaintext copies of Desportes’s sentence. The identification of Gregory XIV belongs to historical interpretation of this accepted wording.

images.caption: The target and earlier manuscript occurrences carrying a PAPE gloss.

notes.title: The Infanta and a French prince
body: The marriage proposal reads “le mariage de l’Infante avec un de nos princes.” The Infanta is accepted as the designation in this passage. Uncertainty about the political arrangement is not an unread cipher word.

The passage follows a request for someone of the House of Bourbon and records refusals and referral to the legate and the Duke of Feria. The translation follows that sequence. It does not silently turn the word “sujet” later in the letter into a firmly identified candidate.

notes.title: Montaigne makes an odd QUI less odd
body: “Moi qui connais les Espagnols, qui me feist…” looks odd if the second QUI must refer to a person. Older French can use a resumptive QUI for a preceding fact, close to modern “ce qui.” Montaigne’s account of actors returning to their humble condition provides a comparison.

That lets the sentence refer back to the writer’s knowledge of the Spaniards without inserting CE into the source. The translation takes that knowledge as the reason for his rejection. The precise scope remains interpretation; the words QUI ME FEIST are accepted.

The nearby S[E]ROIT is a disclosed editorial repair, supported by a complete SEROIT five lines later in the same letter. Montaigne I.1 and Amyot also illustrate older être pour constructions. These works clarify usage; none is a copy of Desportes’s letter. The Montaigne evidence was read in ARTFL’s scholarly transcription, not checked against a sixteenth-century page image.
notes.quote: qui est leur nayfve et originelle condition

notes.title: Once AQU(N) is visible, the word is clear
body: The accepted word is CHAQU(N), modern chacun, across the line break. The surviving AQU(N) and the sentence “au temps que chacun est bandé…” establish the word without leaving it as a substantive alternative.

The initial [ch] remains marked at the damaged edge. This is a final word-level restoration, not a claim that the lost CH strokes have become visible. The distinction lets the readable text be confident while the manuscript record stays accurate.

notes.title: One visual check unlocks a whole word
body: A human reader had identified an H/U-like form where the working transcription favoured E/R. Rechecking that observation against H/U signs on the same line produced B A F / O U E across the line break: bafoué.

No letters needed to be supplied, deleted or replaced editorially. Montaigne’s Essais II.12 uses the participle for derision, supporting the period sense “mocked.” The comparison confirms vocabulary, not the identities of the people doing the mocking.
The abandoned and mocked figure is understood from the longer passage about Mayenne. The period syntax remains compressed; the English makes the implied subject explicit for readability.

refs.label: Montaigne, Essais II.12, displayed p. 450, ARTFL transcription

images.caption: The disputed sign alongside H/U and E/R controls from the manuscript.

notes.quote: Nous n’aurons jamais assez bafoué l’impudence de cet accouplage.

notes.title: Enough to fill eight times the paper
body: The handwritten quantity is accepted as huit in “il y aurait pour en remplir huit tant de papier”: enough to fill eight times as much paper. Exact HUIT/HUICT spelling is a paleographic detail, not a competing numerical reading.
This passage is ordinary cursive, so the paired-letter cipher key cannot decide its strokes. The annotation preserves that distinction from the separate raised-c monetary notation in Frachetta.

notes.title: An intact sign can still be surplus
body: The accepted phrase is “couvrir leurs malices par un monde de faucetés”: cover their malice with a mass of falsehoods. FA- ends one line; UCETES begins the next. The modernized French writes faussetés.

A human visual check established that the E/R sign between DE and FAUCETES is intact. The edition retains it in the source and omits it editorially from the running reading. It is not described as erased, or turned into an extra word.

The A at the edge and U at the next line opening are accepted contextual readings with compatible source forms. The complete word is established; the spare E/R remains a recorded feature of the manuscript.

notes.title: ONT, FONT: listen to the whole sentence
body: Read the whole conditional: “si elle savait … l’artifice de nos amis, ce qu’ils ont, font, leur faiblesse, comme … elle s’étonnerait…” The writer is listing what Your Lordship would know: their methods, what they have and do, their weakness, and how the legate behaved.

FONT selects F from the existing F/S family. Montaigne I.50 supplies a period comparison for juxtaposed finite verbs sharing a subject. It supports the construction, not an exact phrase match. The commas are editorial; no extra conjunction or pronoun is invented.
This is why context must be larger than a pair of neighbouring words. “ONT SONT” is not made better by declaring both words individually legible if it misses the sentence’s structure.

refs.label: Montaigne, Essais I.50, De Democritus et Heraclitus

notes.title: A king he could defend
body: The letter says Mayenne was willing to accept Monsieur Guise as king, provided a means of defending him could be shown. FEIST belongs to “pourvu que l’on lui feist voir”; it is not an invitation to recast the surrounding political claims.
JAMAIS crosses the next line break: its final S appears at the beginning of line 24. Preserving source line breaks exposed a letter that a word-by-word view could easily overlook.

notes.title: Whose expense, whose commands?
body: The closing political argument is readable. Its pronouns still call for interpretation: Desportes proposes communicating the Pope’s intentions to Mayenne without the legate as intermediary, and complains that the legate plays at Mayenne’s expense.

The English follows that contextual assignment of people. It does not claim that every French pronoun names a person independently. The [n] in “il [n]e prendra” remains a disclosed editorial supply. Minor grammar and reference questions do not become additional wholly unread regions.

notes.title: What the brackets mean
body: Square brackets mark editorially supplied or replaced material. [Gondi] is a strong contextual identification whose code remains unproved. Other brackets can mark an accepted missing letter, an abbreviation expansion or the documentary day [22]. They do not all mean the same level of uncertainty.

The original scan is the record of the ink. The historical reading preserves older spelling. The French view modernizes spelling, conventional inflections and word divisions while retaining the wording and source-line correspondence; unusual constructions such as huit tant and en la continue remain. The English gives a readable interpretation and follows the notes where older syntax needs explanation.

Cancelled writing, slashes and the final obelus-like mark remain visible in the manuscript. A cancellation is not deciphered merely by removing it from the running text. Individual hovering follows recorded source units; joined handwriting and some compact abbreviations are intentionally shared regions.

The accepted edition has one substantive unresolved designation, in Frachetta line 26. Aldobrandini has no wholly unread body word in the accepted reading, which includes the disclosed editorial restorations. That is a statement about readable text, not a claim that every pen stroke or historical allegation is settled.

notes.title: Who played the part?
body: The letter reads “nostre docteur Gratian” and says he “a mieulx ioué le personnage que nul des autres”: he played his part better than any of the others. The Recueil Fossard woodcut reproduced here is labelled DOCTOR GRATIAN. That exact title and name, beside the letter’s theatrical language, gives unusually specific support for the reading.

The seven cipher families G E A G I A A permit G R A T I A N without a new sign or supplied letter. GENTIAN fits the pairs too, but lacks this particular title/name/stage-language match. This is an accepted contextual reading, not a claim that the glyphs alone choose every vowel.

Buckley places the print series probably in Paris in the mid-1580s; the print itself is undated. The apparent nickname does not identify a particular actor or diplomat. The nearby SECONDER/SECONDEE ending is a minor E/R choice; the passage’s sense of support by the doctor is established.

refs.label: Recueil Fossard, in Buckley (2009), fig. A30, printed p. 307

images.caption: The DOCTOR GRATIAN label in the Recueil Fossard print, reproduced in Buckley, fig. A30.

notes.title: TANT QUE: a consequence, not a stopwatch
body: The cipher already gives TANT and the QUE sign. The question was how they connect the complaint: to toil, ruin oneself and do everything possible, to such a point that without our prudence things would not last an hour.

In Gargantua, laughter grows so intense that tears come to the characters’ eyes. The quoted TANT QUE introduces that consequence. The parallel supports the older construction and the English “so much so that”; it does not recover erased letters or prove Desportes’s punctuation.
The evidence is the CESR/Renom transcription of the 1534 text, chapter XIX, displayed page [66]. The original printed page was not separately checked for this comparison.
notes.quote: tant que les larmes leurs venoyent es yeulx

notes.title: The final designation
notes.tag: A strong identification, still a supplied name
body: The three uprights occur in “Le voiage de …”. Gondi is the strong contextual identification, specifically the Jérôme / Girolamo Gondi involved in journeys connected with Henry IV’s conversion. The readable edition supplies [Gondi]. The exact name or title encoded by this particular sign has not been independently established.

Henry IV’s letters of 26 April and 30 May 1593 connect a Gondy mission with his Catholic undertaking; the May letter explicitly names Hieronimo de Gondy. Sega’s letter of 26 July associates news of Navarre’s intended declaration with Hieronimo Gondi’s arrival in France.

The latest comparison found a different, looped sign for Cardinal de Gondy in a November 1592 cipher and its readable copy. That is valuable evidence for that letter, but it is not the three-upright sign here. The cardinal and Hieronimo must not be silently conflated.

This is the one remaining substantive designation in the running text. It is not necessary to identify every financial transaction or resolve each grammatical nuance before accepting the rest of the decipherment.

images.caption: The three-upright sign after LE VOIAGE DE.
A different looped sign in the November 1592 comparison. Its value cannot simply be transferred.
The aligned readable copy names Cardinal de Gondy.

notes.title: A tiny raised c, half a million écus
body: Read the group as 5ᶜ, followed by the intact MIL ESCUS. The raised c means hundreds: 5 × 100 × 1,000 = 500,000 écus. The amount is accepted. “Cinq cens” expands two written marks; those words are not eight separate cipher letters.

The S-shaped five was compared with a neighbouring date in the packet. Official palaeography guides document the multiplier convention. Neither a vague visual resemblance nor an attempt to make a historical account add up is the sole basis of the reading.

The verb remains OSTER, “to take away / remove.” The letter does not specify the payer, recipient or exact transaction. In particular, a separate request for 200,000 écus plus Swiss troops does not supply a demonstrated 500,000-écu total.

refs.label: Archives de Meurthe-et-Moselle, historical numerical notation

images.caption: The manuscript’s raised-c quantity before MIL ESCUS.
A five in a nearby dated letter: a form comparison, not a second witness to the amount.

notes.title: “Your humble servant”
body: The Frachetta subscription is accepted at word level as Vostre humble serviteur. The abbreviated Vre, the middle group, and the final servant formula were compared with readable material in the same hand and the related Lisieux letter.

The precise contraction of HUMBLE is not invented in the transcription. The separate lower flourish is a repeated subscription paraph, with no alphabetic expansion assigned. Recognizing a conventional flourish is different from deciding it must spell DESPORTES.

The Aldobrandini farewell preserves Illustrissimo with its visible final O. The distinct abbreviated courtesy Vre Srie Illme expands to Vostre Seigneurie Illustrissime. D. V. S. I. remains in its original abbreviated form.

images.caption: HUMBLE in the comparison letter; expanded wording is distinct from exact contraction.
